short: Sentence decoding from a person who cannot speak holds for 50 words and one participant; the decoder is standard for 2021, and an LM restricted to the test vocabulary drives the gain.
position: The paper changed who is decoded (M04, anarthria; M13, a chronic implant) and moved a closed-vocabulary pipeline from speaking epilepsy patients into that setting (M06, M07); the decoder is standard for 2021 ECoG work, and the advance is the population, rated standard because one participant gives no repetition. The main claim, sentences decoded from a person who cannot speak, holds for 50 words and one participant at 25.6% median WER. The strongest overreach is the language model: trained only on sentences from the test set's 50 words, its drop from 60.5% to 25.6% WER measures a closed-world prior. The no-recalibration claim rests on a post hoc offline analysis of isolated words, not on real-time sentence use. Against today the system is far behind: an intracortical phoneme decoder in a participant with dysarthria reached 99.6% accuracy on 50 words after 30 minutes of recordings [@card2024] ([later]), where this paper collected 22 hours of isolated-word data.

M07: share of the 152 large-vocabulary rescoring studies that are later than 2021 not tallied by year; the review states only that its cited examples [@card2024] and [@metzger2023] are [later].
M04/M13: no topic audit (ledger absence count, deciding priors) exists for chronic use in anarthria; verdicts stay standard under the rules because the effect rests on one participant.
